Internal behavior of domain allocation and handler install and topology lookup and NUMA helpers and fixmap helpers and firmware parsing helpers owned elsewhere.
Lock ordering between ACPI IOAPIC mutex and IOAPIC mutex and domain and IRQ descriptor locks.

findings.text: ACPI GSI registration resolves a global interrupt to a Linux IRQ through the IOAPIC path, translating ACPI trigger and polarity encodings into internal level and active low indications, deriving NUMA affinity from the device when present, protecting lookup and table update with the ACPI IOAPIC mutex, skipping SCI table refresh, and returning either the mapped IRQ or the input GSI when IOAPIC support is absent.
ACPI GSI unregistration re-resolves the global interrupt without allocation attributes under the ACPI IOAPIC mutex and releases the associated IRQ mapping only when a positive IRQ is found.

Allocation descriptors start zeroed with an optional CPU affinity mask, support full copy when a source is supplied and zeroing otherwise, and gain IOAPIC specific type marking plus node and trigger and polarity state with a validity flag when prepared for IOAPIC use.

GSI to IRQ lookup first locates the owning IOAPIC and its pin, optionally enforces that a static routing entry exists when a check flag is set, and then delegates to pin mapping. Legacy status is decided by comparing against the platform legacy count and domain lookup indexes a per IOAPIC table.

Pin mapping rejects the historical cascade interrupt when it arrives through a legacy bus, distinguishes lookup only from allocation paths, reuses an existing domain mapping when present, allocates ISA or generic IRQs otherwise with attribute compatibility checks, and increments a per IRQ sharing count on success.

Attribute completion preserves caller supplied node and trigger and polarity when marked valid, otherwise falls back to firmware override data for the GSI when available, and finally assumes PCI style level and active low signalling.

Attribute compatibility allows a first consumer of a legacy IRQ to reprogram trigger and polarity and refresh the flow handler and stored entry, then requires stored level and active low state to match the requested values.
Handler selection marks level triggered IRQs with level status and uses a fast end of interrupt routine with a matching name, while edge triggered IRQs clear that status and use an edge routine.

IRQ number policy depends on domain kind, with legacy domains reusing low GSIs only after early initialization and otherwise treating them dynamically, strict domains always reusing the GSI, dynamic domains always allocating fresh numbers, and unknown kinds warning and failing.

ISA allocation either attaches an additional IOAPIC pin to an already allocated legacy IRQ after compatibility validation or marks a fresh allocation as legacy and records ISA ownership in chip data. Pin attachment suppresses duplicates and appends a newly allocated list node on a chosen memory node.

The ACPI IOAPIC mutex serializes ACPI GSI registration and unregistration plus IOAPIC hotplug registration and deregistration and presence queries, while a separate IOAPIC mutex serializes pin to IRQ mapping and reference release.

Observed allocation state comprises a type tag, affinity mask, device identifier, flags, and an IOAPIC section carrying node, level indication, active low indication, validity, and pin. Observed chip state comprises sharing count, stored level and polarity in two places, entry copy, ISA marker, and a pin list linked by next pointers.

Mapping lifecycle moves from unmapped to mapped on first allocation with count set, remains mapped with rising count on shared reuse, decrements on unmap, frees the domain allocation when count reaches zero, and never frees ISA owned IRQs through the generic unmap path.

ACPI GSI dispatch defaults to a PIC registration routine with no unregister routine, switches both pointers to IOAPIC routines plus model and presence flags during IOAPIC model setup, and guards unregistration with a null check. Suspend entry defaults to an x86 low level routine in one build variant and stays unresolved in the other.

ACPI CPU mapping converts firmware identifiers to a logical CPU through topology hotplug, applies processor capabilities, records NUMA affinity from firmware handles, and publishes the result. Unmapping clears NUMA affinity and invokes topology hot unplug.

Topology hotplug validates APIC identifier range and prior enumeration, rejects unknown identifiers and exhausted CPU space with distinct errors, records presence, binds firmware and ACPI identifiers to the CPU, and marks primary threads by testing low identifier bits against threads per core. Hot unplug clears mapping and presence unless already invalid, and boot registration records the boot APIC once.

IOAPIC hotplug registration builds a dynamic domain configuration, resolves the IOAPIC identifier from firmware with a UID integer fallback on failure, and registers under the ACPI IOAPIC mutex. Deregistration and presence queries similarly serialize and delegate by GSI base.

IOAPIC deregistration locates the unit by GSI base, vetoes removal when any pin still resolves to an IRQ with a positive sharing count, then clears register count, destroys the IRQ domain, frees saved registers and IO memory reservation, clears the fixmap slot, and zeroes the descriptor.

HPET parsing requires memory space, records address and sequence, ignores empty addresses and repairs a known shifted address on sixty four bit builds depending on a force flag, reserves nine bytes for the firmware resource name, and preallocates a named memory resource spanning a fixed kilobyte block for later insertion. An alternate build disables parsing entirely.

FADT parsing clears legacy device, keyboard controller, RTC, and VGA presence flags according to boot flags and revision, treating newer revisions as authoritative for controller absence and older revisions as using the original timer field, and discovers the PM timer port from extended or legacy fields with selective expansion when the extended field is empty. Boot table parsing saves the CMOS index port for later use.

Early LAPIC setup requires APIC support, parses address override entries with error propagation, records the resulting address once with a one time warning on repeat, establishes a fixed mapping and optionally captures the boot CPU identifier and version, and registers the boot APIC in topology state.

MADT LAPIC enumeration first attempts SAPIC entries and when none appear validates LAPIC presence then enumerates LAPIC and extended APIC entries in firmware order up to a platform limit, requires at least one of the two kinds, and finally parses both NMI kinds with error propagation.

Failure modes include missing IOAPIC or routing entry, cascade reuse, absent domain mapping, attribute mismatch causing busy status, allocation failures from memory or domain limits, removal veto when pins remain shared, invalid APIC range or unenumerated identifier or exhausted CPU capacity, missing IOAPIC identifier, misplaced or empty timer addresses, absent LAPIC support or entries, and repeated boot APIC registration warnings.

GSI addressing adds a per IOAPIC base to the pin index, legacy status holds for non negative IRQs below the platform legacy count, pin iteration spans from zero to the unit register count, and pin list traversal follows standard doubly linked list linkage.

Observed symbolic controls include ACPI edge and level trigger selectors, ACPI active high selectors, IOAPIC allocation and check flags, IOAPIC domain kinds for legacy and strict and dynamic operation, legacy allocation marking, NUMA no node sentinel, MADT entry kinds for override and SAPIC and LAPIC and extended APIC and NMI variants, fixed map slots for IOAPIC and LAPIC bases, and platform limits for local APIC identifiers.
